title: SYSK Selects: How White-collar Crime Works
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of a 2012 episode on white-collar crime. Josh and Chuck open by comparing bank robbery payoffs (UK vs US, study in the journal Significance) with the far greater money in white-collar crime, then define white-collar crime as non-violent occupational deceit and fraud. They survey types: insider trading, securities fraud and stock touting, antitrust violations and price fixing, bribery, embezzlement, money laundering, tax evasion, industrial espionage, environmental crimes, credit card and bankruptcy fraud. They discuss victims being diffuse, the 1473 Carrier's Case as an early white-collar case, the Sherman, Clayton and related antitrust acts, muckrakers, E. A. Ross and his "criminaloid" term, Edwin Sutherland coining "white collar crime" in 1939, the FBI white-collar division in 1974, Sarbanes-Oxley, harsher sentences for figures like Bernie Madoff, RICO, bribery abroad and the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, and Transparency International. The episode ends with listener mail about a charity compilation album and a plug for a Talking Heads song.
topics: bank robbery vs white collar crime

segments.title: Opening banter and bank robbery economics
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the rerun and joke about the sponsor. They discuss a study of bank robberies in the UK and US, finding robbery pays little, and argue that white-collar crime offers far more money with lower risk.

segments.title: Defining white-collar crime
segments.summary: The hosts define white-collar crime as non-violent crime involving deceit and fraud committed through one's occupation, noting it is also called occupational crime and that its definition is hard to pin down.

segments.title: Types of white-collar crime
segments.summary: They list common forms: insider trading, securities fraud, stock manipulation and touting, antitrust violations, price fixing, bribery, embezzlement, money laundering, tax evasion, industrial espionage, and environmental violations.

segments.title: Victims and ethics of white-collar crime
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how white-collar crimes often have diffuse victims who are hard to see, and how corporations may pass losses to employees and consumers.

segments.title: History: Carrier's Case and early antitrust laws
segments.summary: They recount the 1473 Carrier's Case, which led to a law against an act that was not illegal at the time. They then describe the Sherman and Clayton Antitrust Acts, the Jim Crow-era price discrimination, and how these laws were later weakened in enforcement.

segments.title: Muckrakers, E. A. Ross and Sutherland
segments.summary: Muckraking journalists exposed corporate abuses and spurred reforms. E. A. Ross coined the term criminaloid, and Edwin Sutherland coined white collar crime in 1939, arguing that the justice system ignored upper-class crime. Critics later noted problems with his broad definition.
topics: origin of white collar crime term

segments.title: Modern impacts, FBI division and Sarbanes-Oxley
segments.summary: They discuss ripple effects of corporate fraud such as Enron on the stock market, the FBI creating a white-collar crime division in 1974 after falling public trust, the difficulty of detecting these crimes, and the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002.

segments.title: Sentencing, RICO and international bribery
segments.summary: They discuss long sentences such as Bernie Madoff's 150 years, debate whether sentences are fair or deterrent, cover RICO recovery of losses, and describe bribery abroad, the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, and Transparency International.

segments.title: Listener mail and charity album
segments.summary: A listener asks the hosts to promote a charity compilation album of industrial and electronic music, with proceeds going to cancer research. The hosts give contact and social media information.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts close with a Talking Heads song, social media and email contact details, and the podcast's website and network information.
